lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: What is a [JWT|J W T|c]? And is it safe to use?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: A [JWT|J W T|c] is a signed note from the server. It says: this is user forty two.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It is very useful, but also easy to misuse. So let us look at both sides.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Here is a real token. It looks random, but it has two dots.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The dots split it into three parts. The header.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The payload.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And the signature.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The header and payload are just JSON, encoded as base sixty four.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The header says which algorithm signed it: [HS256|H S two fifty six|c].

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The payload holds the claims. [sub|sub|c] is the user. [role|role|c] is what they may do.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And [exp|exp|c] is when the token expires: fifteen minutes after it was issued.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Did you need a key to read all that?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: No. Anyone with the token can read it. A [JWT|J W T|c] is signed, not secret.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Then what stops me from changing it?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The signature. The server feeds the header, the payload, and its secret key into [HMAC|H MAC|c].

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Out comes the signature. Only someone with the key can make one that matches.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Now, a real login. Your app sends your email and password.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The server checks them, signs a token, and sends it back.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Your app sends that token with every request, in the Authorization header.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The server recomputes the signature, and checks the expiry. No database lookup needed.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Let us try to cheat. We change the role from user to admin.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The server recomputes the signature from the edited payload. It does not match.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: So the token is rejected. Without the key, you cannot forge a signature.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So why is it so popular?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The server stays stateless, and any service with the key can check the token by itself.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: And what is the catch?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Catch one: you cannot take a token back.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: A user logs out at ten. But a copied token still works until it expires, at ten fifteen.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Catch two: claims go stale.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The role changes to editor in the database, but the token still says user.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Catch three: size. A session id is thirty two characters. Our token is two hundred thirty five, and it grows with every claim.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Catch four: in local storage, one cross site scripting bug lets a script steal the token.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Now, the mistakes to avoid.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: One: trusting the algorithm in the header. An attacker sets [alg|alg|c] to [none|none|c], meaning no signature.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: A careless verifier skips the check, and accepts a fake admin token.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The fix: pin the algorithm on the server, and reject anything else.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Pinning also stops key confusion, where a public key is misused as the secret.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Two: a weak secret. With one token, an attacker guesses offline.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Our test secret fell on the fifth guess. Use at least thirty two random bytes.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Three: skipping checks. Always check expiry, issuer, and audience.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Four: secrets in the payload. Remember, anyone can read it.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So what should I do instead?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Keep access tokens short: five to fifteen minutes.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Keep the refresh token in an [HttpOnly|HTTP only|c] cookie, so scripts cannot read it.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Rotate it on every use. If an old one comes back, it was stolen.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And for a single server, a classic session is simpler, and easy to revoke.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So a [JWT|J W T|c] is a tool, not a default.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Exactly. Signed, not secret. Short lived. Verified strictly.
